parts: Lesson 29: Cleaning and Cleaning Materials (Module 6A, lesson 29) — Summary

Cleaning is removing dust, dirt and undesirable materials (stains, spots) by dusting, shaking, sweeping, mopping, washing or polishing, scrubbing, disinfecting and rearranging. Without regular cleaning the house becomes a breeding ground for cockroaches, ants, flies and mosquitoes and causes asthma and bronchitis; cleaning gives a good appearance, comfort and hygiene. Dust is loose particles easily moved by air that settle on surfaces and are removed with a dry cloth; dirt is dust that sticks to a surface with moisture or grease and needs a detergent.

Dusting: wiping with a dry clean soft cloth. Shaking and beating: carpets, rugs and curtains in open air. Sweeping: a broom carries dust along; walls from top downward; floors from one end to the door; lift movable articles. Mopping: wiping with a damp coarse cloth, paying attention to nooks and corners. Washing: scrubbing with a yard (bamboo) broom and plenty of water, with detergent for tough dirt. Polishing: rubbing a polish on a surface to bring out a shine.

Equipment: dusters (soft cotton or flannel; separate ones for the dining table, mirrors and kitchen slabs; wash after use), dust pans, mops (thick loosely woven cotton; squeeze, change water after each room, wash and dry after use), polishing cloth (flannel), brooms (soft for sweeping; hard yard broom for washing), brushes (nylon for carpets and furniture, round feather brush for cobwebs, metal for wire mesh, special for toilets), buckets, dust bins (plastic with lid, lined with paper, emptied and washed daily) and the vacuum cleaner (sucks dust into a disposable bag). Materials: water; detergents (with surfactants; should dissolve readily, work in all water, give good wetting and suspending power, be harmless, clean quickly and rinse away easily; scum is the grey film left by cheap soaps); abrasives (sand, powdered brick, sawdust, wheat bran, emery paper, fine ash, steel wool, coconut fibre); acids (strong acids for toilets, milder for dirty tiles; vinegar and lemon for brass and copper stains); alkalis (baking soda and ammonia are grease emulsifiers); bleaches (sodium hypochlorite, sodium perborate, hydrogen peroxide); solvents (methylated spirit, carbon tetrachloride, kerosene and petrol remove grease and wax; inflammable; carbon tetrachloride is harmful if inhaled); and polishes (furniture cream of beeswax and turpentine, furniture polish of linseed oil, turpentine, vinegar and methylated spirit, metal polish with soap, ammonia and bath brick, copper cleaner of fine sand, flour, salt and vinegar). Polish principles: remove dust and dirt first, use small quantities, rub off thoroughly, and polish permanently polished surfaces carefully.

Daily clean, weekly clean (more thorough) and spring (annual) clean (most thorough). Daily clean of a room: open windows, remove unwanted articles and empty ash trays and dust bins, sweep, dust, brush or vacuum the carpet, mop, replace linen and make a final survey. Kitchen daily: collect utensils, wipe the stove, appliances and counters, wash utensils, sweep, empty and line the dustbin and mop with a mild disinfectant. Weekly: remove stains from walls and doors, clean drawers, fittings, pictures and lights, vacuum carpets, change linen; kitchen: empty shelves, clean jars and bins, change newspapers, clean tiles. Spring cleaning: ventilate, remove linen and curtains and all movable articles, clean cobwebs, do maintenance, polish furniture and floors, clean carpets in the sun or dry clean; kitchen: spread pulses in the sun, clean exhaust fan and switches, wash tiles with detergent, spray insecticides, tighten screws and wash the floor.
